primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'harvest' primarily symbolizes the eschatological ingathering of people at the end of the age — God's final gathering of the righteous into His kingdom and the corresponding judgment of the wicked. Jesus explicitly interprets the figure this way ('the harvest is the end of the age'), and the image carries a dual aspect: salvation/gathering of God's people (wheat into the barn) and judgment/destruction of the unrighteous (weeds burned, grapes trodden in the winepress).
primary_basis: Matthew 13:24-30, 36-43 (parable of the wheat and weeds; 'the harvest is the end of the age, and the harvesters are angels')
Revelation 14:14-20 (the Son of Man reaping the earth with a sickle; the grape harvest and winepress of God's wrath)
Joel 3:13 ('Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe' — judgment of the nations)
Matthew 3:12 / Luke 3:17 (John the Baptist: gathering wheat into the barn, burning the chaff)
Mark 4:26-29 (parable of the growing seed; sickle put in when grain is ripe)
Jeremiah 51:33 and Hosea 6:11 (harvest as appointed time of judgment/restoration)

alternatives.meaning: Evangelistic/missionary harvest: people who are spiritually ready to receive the gospel, with believers as 'workers' sent to gather them. This is extremely widespread in preaching and missions literature ('the harvest is plentiful but the workers are few') and in some traditions functions as the default meaning of 'the harvest.'
basis: John 4:35-38 ('the fields are ripe for harvest')

alternatives.meaning: Moral principle of sowing and reaping: harvest as the inevitable consequence or reward of one's conduct — one reaps what one sows, whether righteousness or corruption.

Firstfruits/resurrection typology: Christ's resurrection as the 'firstfruits' of a larger harvest of resurrected believers; the Old Testament harvest feasts (Firstfruits, Weeks/Pentecost, Ingathering/Tabernacles) read typologically as stages of God's redemptive plan.
basis: Acts 2 (Pentecost as harvest-feast fulfillment in some typological readings)

alternatives.meaning: Harvest (or its failure) as a sign of covenant blessing or curse: abundant harvest signifying God's favor and provision; blighted or lost harvest signifying divine discipline.
Missed harvest as an image of lost opportunity for salvation or repentance.
basis: Jeremiah 8:20 ('The harvest is past, the summer has ended, and we are not saved')

notes: The symbolism of 'harvest' is well established but genuinely twofold at the top level. Scholarly and doctrinal treatments most often anchor the symbol in the eschatological end-of-the-age gathering and judgment (Matthew 13; Revelation 14; Joel 3), while popular preaching and missions usage most often anchors it in the evangelistic 'harvest of souls' (Matthew 9; John 4). These two strands are closely related — the mission harvest is frequently framed as the present-tense outworking of the end-time ingathering — so most interpreters treat them as complementary rather than competing. The sowing-and-reaping moral principle and the firstfruits/resurrection typology are distinct but widely recognized secondary uses. No major Christian tradition disputes the basic symbolic field; disagreements concern emphasis (judgment vs. salvation vs. mission) rather than the meaning itself.
